title: Among 505 earthquakes in 1995-2026, only Denali 2002 (119 kPa) changed Yellowstone geyser intervals; ten events at 16-38 kPa long-period stress gave no detectable change
abstract: Question: do Yellowstone geyser eruption intervals change after earthquakes more than at placebo times, and which shaking measure predicts a change? We used 14 regular geysers from the GeyserTimes archive (1995-2026) and 567 declustered earthquakes from USGS ComCat. For each earthquake, we measured the long-period (0.01-0.4 Hz) peak ground velocity at broadband stations near Yellowstone (median of up to five stations) and converted it to peak dynamic stress. For each geyser, we compared the 7-day median interval after the event with the 7-day median before it, and calibrated the change with about 700 placebo dates within one year. The plan was written before the analysis; three amendments are reported. Result: the 2002 M7.9 Denali earthquake (119 kPa) is the only clear response (event p = 0.005; rank-based p = 0.021). Daisy intervals became 38% shorter and Castle intervals became 12% longer, as Husen et al. (2004) reported. Daisy returned to the band of 29 other years in week 9. The ten next-largest stresses (16-38 kPa, including Michoacan 2022, Ridgecrest 2019, Stanley 2020 and Tehuantepec 2017) gave placebo p from 0.31 to 0.93 (combined p = 0.91). Over 317 events, -log10 p had no correlation with long-period stress (rho = -0.04), local broadband velocity or the Wang (2007) energy density. Only 16 of 505 scored events had p < 0.05, against 25 expected. Thus the data support a response threshold above 38 kPa for changes larger than about 7-15% in the most regular geysers. Main limitation: Denali is the only event above 40 kPa, so the threshold between 38 and 119 kPa is not located, and seasonal gaps reduce the number of geysers for winter events.
